mioc-001.title: Africa's plants lose ground to the seasons
mioc-001.text: Africa's plant life took a sharp hit as the Miocene began. Plant diversity fell steeply, probably because the seasons became more pronounced, with stronger swings between wet and dry. Species suited to steady conditions lost out. The great equatorial forest belt did not simply shrink. Through the whole Miocene it broke apart and rejoined again and again, splitting forest populations and then reconnecting them.

mioc-003.title: Apes spread across the Old World
mioc-003.text: Morotopithecus, about 21.6 million years old, carries the earliest claimed upright spine and vertical body plan of any ape. It belongs to a group just finding its feet. Apes first evolved in the early Miocene, in the Aquitanian and Burdigalian ages, and then diversified and spread across the Old World. Geography made the spread possible. Once Afro-Arabia met Eurasia, hominoids, the ape group, and proboscideans, the elephant group, could walk out of Africa. Apes crossed in waves. Griphopithecus lived in Turkey and Slovakia 15–13.5 million years ago, and Dryopithecus had reached Europe by 12.5 million years ago. One proposal, the 'Out-of-Europe' idea, holds that several great ape species evolved in Eurasia during the Miocene. The crossing itself is the subject of {{ref:mioc-037}}, and the later story of the apes runs through {{ref:mioc-046}} to the split of human and chimpanzee lines.

mioc-004.title: Himalayan rubble builds the Bengal Fan
mioc-004.text: The largest submarine fan on Earth lies under the Bay of Bengal: about 3,000 km long, 1,430 km wide and up to 16.5 km thick. It is made of mountains. Sediment eroded from the rising Himalaya and Tibetan Plateau, carried mostly by the Ganges and Brahmaputra, built the Bengal Fan. The oldest sediments recovered from it so far are Early Miocene, so the fan is at least that old. Their minerals and chemistry point to Himalayan origin. So the Himalaya was already a major mountain range 20 million years ago. The fan keeps a running diary of the uplift, and changes in its layers show that Himalayan uplift slowed in the Late Pliocene.

mioc-006.title: The daisy family takes off
mioc-006.text: With over 32,000 species, about 10% of all flowering plants, the daisy family rivals the orchids as the largest plant family. The geologic time scale lists it as appearing and diversifying rapidly in the Early Miocene, triggering radiations of rodents, snakes and songbirds. Its roots are older: its oldest fossil pollen, from Antarctica, is 76-66 million years old.

mioc-007.title: The East Asian summer monsoon takes modern shape
mioc-007.text: Global cooling led the East Asian Summer Monsoon to begin taking its modern form in the Early Miocene. The mountains mattered too. Major phases of Himalayan geology during the Miocene changed Asian monsoon patterns. Those patterns were tied in turn to glacial periods in the north, so ice far away and rock nearby both shaped the rain. The link between rising Tibet and stronger monsoons, first seen in {{ref:olig-063}}, keeps returning through the Neogene.

mioc-018.title: Tian Shan and Altai rise in Central Asia
mioc-018.text: India's collision with Eurasia reached far north. The geologic time scale lists the Tian Shan and Altai Mountains as forming in the Early Miocene, as part of the Himalayan orogeny. The Siberian Altai is the northernmost region the collision affected. The Tian Shan rose sharply again in the Late Miocene, blocking westerly winds from the Tarim Basin and drying it.

mioc-002.title: The Andes rise fastest in the Miocene
mioc-002.text: The new Nazca Plate dove head-on under South America, and the Andes rose, most of all in the Miocene. The Altiplano began rising in this epoch. By about 13–11 million years ago it was a high plateau, second in size only to Tibet. From the Late Miocene the Altiplano region climbed from low elevations to over 3,000 m. Peru's Western Cordillera, quiet since the Oligocene, rose sharply after about 10 Ma. The uplift ran the length of the range. The Principal Cordillera east of Santiago rose about 20–8 Ma, and Colombia's Eastern Ranges were lifted and eroded faster 12–3 Ma. Near Misti, the Western Cordillera rose 9–4 Ma amid large ignimbrites. Movement on the Atacama Fault raised the Chilean Coast Range, and the Quechua phases of 9–8 and 7–5 Ma deformed northern Peru.

mioc-005.title: Whales and dolphins at their most diverse
mioc-005.text: The Miocene ocean held over 20 genera of baleen whales. Only six survive today. Whales and dolphins were at their most diverse in this epoch. The boom in baleen whales brought its own hunters: raptorial sperm whales, toothed whales with large biting teeth, apparently evolved to prey on them. From around 15 million years ago, modern cetaceans began to reach enormous sizes. One of those whale-hunters, Livyatan, appears in {{ref:mioc-125}}.

mioc-008.title: The Fram Strait opens a door to the Arctic
mioc-008.text: The Arctic Ocean got one entrance from the Atlantic, and only one. The Fram Strait opened in the Miocene and became the only route for Atlantic water into the Arctic until the Quaternary. Another path existed on the map, the Barents Seaway, but uplift of the continental shelf kept the water from passing through it.

mioc-009.title: Diatoms move into fresh water
mioc-009.text: Diatoms, single-celled algae in glassy shells, had radiated in the oceans back in the Cretaceous. Freshwater diatoms did not appear until the Miocene. Their diversity rose through the epoch as carbon dioxide and global temperatures fell.

mioc-010.title: Grass takes over the world
mioc-010.text: Grass did not just spread in the Miocene. It changed the climate that let it spread. As in the Oligocene, grasses kept advancing and came to dominate much of the world while forests dwindled. Early Miocene forests gave way to mixed forest and grassland in the Middle Miocene. Oregon was savanna by 12 Ma, and grasslands and savannas were established by about 10 Ma. The new grasses were fibrous and fire-tolerant. They co-evolved with herds of grazers that had high-crowned teeth, and those herds displaced woodland and browsing animals. By the Hemingfordian age, savanna dominated North America and grazing horses outnumbered browsers. Ants, termites, grassland mammals and snakes diversified. A cooler, drier climate and open landscapes were a major cause of the decline of perissodactyls, the odd-toed hoofed mammals. Then came the feedback. Deep grassland soils buried carbon and held water, and pale grass raised albedo, the share of sunlight reflected. Both helped make the climate cooler and drier still.

mioc-011.title: Kelp forests rise in Miocene seas
mioc-011.text: Two new biomes carried much of Miocene life. One was the grassland. The other grew underwater. Kelp forests, dense stands of giant brown seaweed, first appeared in Miocene seas and soon became one of Earth's most productive ecosystems. On land and in the sea, then, the epoch built new kinds of habitat at the same time, each feeding a great range of animals.

mioc-012.title: Necrolestes, last of an ancient line
mioc-012.text: Meridiolestidans were mammals that dominated Late Cretaceous South America. Their last member turned up in the Miocene of Patagonia: Necrolestes, a mole-like burrowing insect-eater. It appears 50 million years after the previous known member of its group, a very long silence in the record.

mioc-013.title: Ducks, owls and crows: modern birds appear
mioc-013.text: Many birds that would look familiar today show up in the Miocene. Clearly recognisable dabbling ducks, plovers, typical owls, cockatoos and crows all appear in this epoch. Crows of the genus Corvus are first recorded about 17 million years ago. By the end of the Miocene, all or nearly all modern bird groups are thought to have been present.

mioc-015.title: Sloth families multiply
mioc-015.text: Sloths diversified in the Miocene, when the major sloth families appeared. Their diversity rose and fell through the epoch and then declined at its end. They had already traveled far: a basal sloth group had colonized the Antilles by the early Miocene.

mioc-016.title: Snakes boom in North America
mioc-016.text: Snakes had been a minor part of North American wildlife. In the Miocene their numbers and diversity rose sharply. Vipers and elapids, the cobra family, first appeared on the continent, and colubrids diversified into many modern genera. The spread of grassland in {{ref:mioc-010}} helped them.

mioc-017.title: South America's native hoofed mammals thin out
mioc-017.text: Notoungulates lost 45% of their families during the Miocene, though their number of species stayed stable. Fewer branches carried as many leaves. By the late Miocene, litopterns and notoungulates were the only South American native ungulate groups still standing.

mioc-014.title: The Ogallala spreads its gravels over the Plains
mioc-014.text: As the Rockies rose, rivers carried eroded rock east and dumped sand and gravel across the gentle plains in overlapping alluvial fans, fan-shaped spreads of river sediment. These deposits form the Ogallala Formation. They hold the Ogallala Aquifer, one of the world's largest, under about 450,000 km2 of eight states, supplying about 30% of US irrigation groundwater.

mioc-019.title: Riversleigh's rainforest animals
mioc-019.text: Riversleigh's limestone never compacted, so its bones stay three-dimensional. In the Early Miocene, Faunal Zone B, the area was very wet rainforest. Later Middle Miocene layers hold a 15-million-year-old platypus relative, Obdurodon, and the oldest modern bandicoots and bilbies.

mioc-021.title: The Central Andes begin erupting ignimbrites
mioc-021.text: Ignimbrite is rock made from a glowing avalanche of volcanic ash that welds as it settles. About 23 million years ago, large-scale ignimbrite volcanism began in the Central Andes, and it continues today. North of 21 degrees S, the Oxaya Formation erupted 23 to 18 million years ago. Calderas of the Altiplano-Puna complex have since produced about 15,000 cubic km of ignimbrite, mostly dacite. One early eruption, the Verde Ignimbrite from Aguas Calientes caldera 17.2 million years ago, released 140–300 cubic km. In southern Peru, the Chuquibamba Ignimbrite came from a VEI 7 super-eruption 14.3 to 13.2 million years ago.

mioc-025.title: Foulden Maar, a forest in a crater lake
mioc-025.text: A small crater lake in New Zealand became a fossil archive. Layers of diatomite, rock built from the shells of countless diatoms, settled on its floor. They preserved fish, plants, spiders, insects and pollen from the subtropical forest around the lake.

mioc-026.title: An impact gouges the Karakul crater
mioc-026.text: A large impact gouged the 52 km Karakul crater in Tajikistan. Its age is poorly pinned. Estimates put it at less than 23 million years, possibly less than 5 million years, so it formed during either the Miocene or the Pliocene.

mioc-027.title: Megalodon, the giant shark, appears
mioc-027.text: The giant shark megalodon evolved around 23 million years ago, by the usual reckoning. With the sperm whale Livyatan, it was among the large predators that ruled Neogene oceans. Its first appearance is disputed. Some remains are reported from about 28 million years ago, while other estimates are as young as 16 million years.

mioc-024.title: Ebelsberg preserves the Paratethys sea life
mioc-024.text: In Upper Austria, a deposit from the Aquitanian age holds a crowded snapshot of the central Paratethys Sea. It preserves huge numbers of plants, fish, marine mammals and invertebrates, the life of the inland sea described in {{ref:olig-015}}.

mioc-020.title: The Alboran Basin and the Betic Corridor open
mioc-020.text: Between 23 and 20 million years ago, spreading thinned the crust south of Spain to just 12-15 km, forming the Alboran Basin. In the early Miocene Iberia rotated and opened the Betic Corridor, a strait joining the Mediterranean and the Atlantic. Its fate matters later, in {{ref:mioc-154}}.

mioc-022.title: Chiapas amber traps a Mexican forest
mioc-022.text: Resin from trees in Chiapas, Mexico, hardened into amber with life caught inside. It holds insects, other arthropods, plant fragments and even the fungi that grew on leaf surfaces, a fine-grained record of a Miocene forest floor and canopy.

mioc-023.title: East Antarctic glaciers come and go
mioc-023.text: East Antarctica probably held some glaciers during the early to mid Miocene, 23 to 15 million years ago. They were restless. The Ross Sea margin of the East Antarctic Ice Sheet advanced and retreated often during the Early Miocene, ice that had not yet settled into a stable cap.
